checks.claim: Independently generated channels' information about shared X adds without redundancy.
checks.explanation: Conditional independence given \(X\) does not remove the information that outputs share with each other. That redundancy must be subtracted. Marginal output independence alone is insufficient as well, because synergistic information can appear only in their joint observation.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(X\) be a fair bit and \(Y_i=X\oplus N_i\), where \(N_1,N_2\) are independent Bernoulli noises with probability \(0.1\), independent of \(X\). The channels are conditionally independent and every conditional output has positive probability. Writing \(h_2\) for binary entropy in bits,

\[
I(X;Y_i)=1-h_2(0.1)\approx0.5310044,
\]

whereas

\[
I(X;Y_1,Y_2)=1+h_2(0.18)-2h_2(0.1)\approx0.7420859<1.0620088.
\]

Thus two independent randomized channels do not contribute the sum of their separate informations. If independence is instead interpreted marginally, take independent fair bits \(Y_1,Y_2\) and \(X=Y_1\oplus Y_2\): individual information is zero but joint information is one bit.
checks.repair:
Keep the chain rule. Under conditional independence, the exact replacement is

\[
I(X;Y_{1:d})=\sum_i I(X;Y_i)-\operatorname{TC}(Y_{1:d}),\qquad
\operatorname{TC}(Y_{1:d})=\sum_iH(Y_i)-H(Y_{1:d})\geq0.
\]

Expanding the mutual informations and using \(H(Y_{1:d}\mid X)=\sum_iH(Y_i\mid X)\) proves this identity. Additivity follows if output total correlation also vanishes. For example, independent components of \(X\) revealed by separate channels satisfy that stronger condition.
checks.scope: The chain rule in Equation (14) remains correct. Equation (15) needs the redundancy term before it can describe the information supplied by conditionally independent channels about a shared input.
checks.claimContext: Appendix M.3 passes from the mutual-information chain rule to additivity for independent channels about the same input \(X\). Independent model randomness is offered as a reason for that independence.
checks.title: Independent channel randomness does not make shared-input information additive
checks.whyItMatters: The claimed additive information justification for diversity combining fails; adding a channel can provide less new information than its individual mutual information.

checks.demonstration:
Take \(n=p=2\), \(G=I\), \(v=e_1\), and \(\Sigma(t)=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha(t),10)\), with \(\alpha(t)=1/(1-t)\) for \(0\le t<1\). All stated coupling and bounded-background assumptions hold exactly, but \(\operatorname{SHC}=(\alpha-10)^2/4\) decreases for \(1\le\alpha<10\).

Even an eventual claim fails if the second variance is \(2+\sin(\alpha^3)\). At arbitrarily large \(\alpha_k=(2\pi k)^{1/3}>2\),
\[
\left.\frac{d\,\operatorname{SHC}}{d\alpha}\right|_{\alpha=\alpha_k}=\frac{(\alpha_k-2)(1-3\alpha_k^2)}2<0.
\]
The background remains positive and bounded. Its derivative need not be bounded or negligible.
checks.repair:
For \(n\ge2\), fixed \(u\ne0\), and bounded background \(C_\perp(\alpha)\), write \(R=uu^\top\) and \(A^\circ=A-\operatorname{tr}(A)I/n\). Then
\[
\operatorname{SHC}(\alpha R+C_\perp)=\frac{\alpha^2\|R^\circ\|_F^2}{n}+O(\alpha),
\]
which proves divergence as \(\alpha\to\infty\). If the background is constant,
\[
\frac{d}{d\alpha}\operatorname{SHC}(\alpha R+C_\perp)=\frac{2}{n}\left[\alpha\|R^\circ\|_F^2+\langle R^\circ,C_\perp^\circ\rangle_F\right],
\]
which is positive beyond an explicit threshold. Bounded background with \(dC_\perp/d\alpha=o(1)\) also gives an eventually positive derivative with respect to \(\alpha\).

Strict time monotonicity additionally requires strictly increasing \(\alpha(t)\) in that regime. If \(\alpha(t)\) is merely nondecreasing, the corresponding time conclusion is nondecreasing.

\[\dot z=W(p)\operatorname{ReLU}(z)+(0,p)^\top,\qquad W(p)=\begin{pmatrix}-1&p\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.\]

The fixed point is \(z^*(p)=(p^2,p)^\top\), lies strictly inside that orthant, and has local Jacobian \(J=W(p)\). Hence

primal-dual-decoding-one-step-bound.summary: A one-step decoder samples before its multiplier update, so its expected deficit can stay positive as the dual step size increases. checks.location: Statement 1; Algorithm 1 lines 3-7; Appendix A.5 Eq. (58)
checks.claim: For every eta>0 a feasible problem has expected constraint violation O(log((eta+1)/(b_max-R/L))/eta).
checks.explanation: With one reverse step, the final sample depends on the initial multiplier but not on the subsequent step-size-dependent update. Its expected deficit can remain strictly positive for every \(\eta\), contradicting a bound that vanishes as \(\eta\) grows.
checks.demonstration:
Take one position, three tokens with base probabilities \(p=(0.6,0.3,0.1)\), contributions \(b=(0,0.4,1)\), target \(R=0.7\), and initial multiplier \(\lambda_T=1\). The sampling rule gives
\[q_j=\frac{p_je^{b_j}}{\sum_kp_ke^{b_k}}\approx(0.454761,0.339212,0.206028).\]
Thus \(\mathbb E_q[b]\approx0.341713\) and the signed expected deficit is \(0.358287\), independently of \(\eta\). The comparator \((0.05,0.05,0.9)\) has expected contribution \(0.92>R\), positive support and finite KL, so the problem is strictly feasible. The one-step process is Markov and absorbing, with finite logits.
At \(\eta=10000\), Eq. (58) gives approximately \(0.00109976\), below the actual deficit. Increasing \(\eta\) further reduces the claimed bound without changing the sample. There is no remaining step on which the updated multiplier could act.
checks.repair:
A finite-step guarantee must retain an initialization or optimization-error term unless the multiplier is adjusted before the irreversible sample. For a one-position finite-token model with positive base probabilities and \(R<b_{\max}\), a valid pre-sampling repair is to choose \(\lambda\) until the tilted law satisfies \(\mathbb E_{q_\lambda}[b]\ge R\). Indeed,
\[\frac{d}{d\lambda}\mathbb E_{q_\lambda}[b]=\operatorname{Var}_{q_\lambda}(b)\ge0,\qquad\mathbb E_{q_\lambda}[b]\longrightarrow b_{\max}.\]
Hence a finite such \(\lambda\) exists. This proves feasibility for the repaired one-position expected-constraint problem, not the original finite-step rate or almost-sure feasibility of a sampled token. A multi-step guarantee needs to account for previous irreversible commitments.
